title: Formal Letter Writing — editor, application, complaint, inquiry
topicTitle: Formal Letter Writing — editor, application, complaint, inquiry
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you do NOT know (editor, manager, office). Half the marks are the fixed BLOCK LAYOUT; the other half is polite business tone.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Recipient's designation + address → Subject line → Salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam') → Body (3 short paragraphs: who you are + purpose / details / polite request) → Complimentary close → Signature + full name in capitals.
**The pairing rule that trips everyone:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' → end **Yours faithfully**; 'Dear Mr/Ms Sharma' (real name) → end **Yours sincerely**.
**Tone grammar:** no contractions (*do not*, *I am*); polite modals (*would*, *could*, *may*); passive voice for formality ('the matter is being investigated').

**Variants:** *Editor* (public issue + call for action), *Job application* (post + skills + 'Enclosure: CV'), *Complaint* (what, when, defect + remedy + deadline), *Inquiry/Order* (price/availability/terms).
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete block format template:**
[Your Address]
[City, Postal Code]
[Date: 15 March 2025]

[Recipient's Designation]
[Recipient's Organisation]
[Recipient's Address]

Subject: [Clear, specific subject line — 5-8 words]

Dear Sir/Madam,

Paragraph 1: State who you are and why you are writing. Be concise.

Paragraph 2: Provide details, facts, or supporting information. Use formal tone.

Paragraph 3: State your request, expectation, or call to action clearly.

Yours faithfully,

[Signature]
[YOUR FULL NAME IN CAPITALS]

**Letter to the Editor — structure and strategy:** Purpose: highlight a public issue, propose action, influence opinion. Opening: 'Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw attention to…' Body: State the issue (what, where, when), its impact (who suffers, how severely), and evidence (facts, observations). Closing: 'I urge the concerned authorities to…' or 'I hope the authorities will take immediate action.' Key: be constructive, not just critical. Offer a solution. Word limit: 120-150 words. No 'Enclosure' line.

**Job Application / Cover Letter — structure and strategy:** Purpose: apply for an advertised position. Opening: 'With reference to your advertisement in [newspaper/portal] dated [date] for the post of [title], I wish to apply…' Body paragraph 1: Your qualifications and relevant experience. Body paragraph 2: Skills matching the job requirements, soft skills, availability. Closing: 'I have enclosed my CV and certificates for your consideration. I am available for an interview at your convenience.' End with 'Enclosure: 1. Curriculum Vitae 2. Copies of certificates 3. Passport-size photograph'. Address the letter to a specific person if possible (e.g., 'The Human Resources Manager').

**Complaint Letter — structure and strategy:** Purpose: report a problem and demand resolution. Opening: 'I am writing to complain about [product/service] purchased on [date] from [place].' Body paragraph 1: Describe the problem factually — what happened, when, model/serial number, receipt details. Body paragraph 2: State the impact (inconvenience, financial loss, safety risk). Body paragraph 3: Specify the remedy you expect (repair, replacement, refund, compensation) and a reasonable deadline. Closing: 'I expect a resolution within [7/14] days. If the matter is not resolved, I will escalate to the consumer forum.' Attach copies of receipts, warranty cards. Tone: firm but polite — never abusive.

**Inquiry / Order Letter — structure and strategy:** Purpose: ask for information or place an order. Opening: 'I am writing to inquire about…' / 'I would like to place an order for…' Body: For inquiries — list specific questions (price, discount, delivery time, warranty, payment terms). For orders — provide item details (name, quantity, specifications, model numbers). Closing: 'Please send the information at your earliest convenience' / 'Please confirm the order and expected delivery date.' Include your contact details for reply. If ordering, mention payment method (cheque enclosed / online payment reference).

**Formal letter vocabulary — power words:** Instead of 'I want', use 'I would like to request'; instead of 'You must', use 'I would be grateful if you could'; instead of 'This is wrong', use 'This appears to be an error'; instead of 'Fix it', use 'Kindly rectify the issue'; instead of 'Tell me', use 'Please inform me'; instead of 'Send me', use 'Kindly dispatch'; instead of 'I need', use 'I require'. These shifts demonstrate command of formal register.

**Common formal letter errors in exams:** (1) Wrong salutation/close pairing: 'Dear Sir' + 'Yours sincerely' (should be 'Yours faithfully'). (2) Missing subject line — examiners deduct marks. (3) Informal contractions: 'I'm', 'don't', 'can't'. (4) Emotional language: 'This is terrible', 'I'm furious'. (5) Vague subject: 'Complaint' (should be 'Complaint regarding defective refrigerator — Model XYZ'). (6) No date or wrong date format. (7) Forgetting 'Enclosure' line when documents are attached. (8) Using 'I' excessively — passive voice preferred for objectivity. (9) Exceeding word limit. (10) No signature line.

**Formal letter punctuation rules:** (1) No punctuation after sender's address lines, date, recipient's address lines, subject line, salutation (just 'Dear Sir/Madam,'), complimentary close ('Yours faithfully,'), or name. (2) The body paragraphs use normal sentence punctuation. (3) In 'Enclosure:', the colon is followed by a list, each item on a new line. (4) If using 'Ref:' or 'Re:', place it before the subject line. (5) Pin code / ZIP code on the last line of the address.

**Addressing envelopes — exam vs. real life:** In exams, you write the letter content only — no envelope. In real life: Sender's address on top-left of back flap. Recipient's address centred on front. Stamp top-right. For official letters: 'To, The Principal, [School Name], [Address]' on front. If using window envelope, ensure recipient's address shows through the window. Postage: check current rates for weight.

**RTI (Right to Information) letter format:** Special formal letter to government offices. Subject: 'Application under Section 6(1) of RTI Act, 2005'. Address to 'Public Information Officer'. Body: specific questions numbered. Fee: ₹10 postal order attached (mention 'Postal Order No. XXXXX dated XXXXX enclosed'). Closing: 'Kindly provide the information within 30 days as per the Act.' This format is increasingly asked in competitive exams.

**Email vs. formal letter — key differences:** Email has To/CC/BCC fields, subject line is mandatory, no sender's address block, no complimentary close signature block (just name). But tone, structure, and grammar rules are IDENTICAL. In exams, if asked to write an email, use the formal letter body structure but add 'To:' and 'Subject:' fields at the top. Do not write 'Dear Sir/Madam,' in the subject line — it goes in the body.
confusion: Yours faithfully vs. Yours sincerely: Use 'Yours faithfully' when you DON'T know the recipient's name (Dear Sir/Madam). Use 'Yours sincerely' when you DO know the name (Dear Mr. Sharma). This is the #1 tested rule in formal letters. Mnemonic: 'Faithful to strangers, sincere to names.'

Subject line vs. Salutation: The subject line is a brief summary (5-8 words) placed BEFORE the salutation. The salutation is the greeting ('Dear Sir/Madam,'). Some students write 'Subject: Dear Sir' — this is wrong. Subject: 'Complaint about damaged goods'. Salutation: 'Dear Sir/Madam,'.

Complaint letter vs. Angry letter: A complaint letter states facts, impact, and desired remedy calmly. An angry letter uses emotional language, threats, and insults. Examiners reward the former; they penalise the latter. 'I am disappointed' is formal; 'This is rubbish' is not.

Enclosure vs. Attachment: In a physical letter, write 'Enclosure: CV' at the bottom. In an email, write 'Attachment: CV.pdf' or simply attach the file. Do not write 'Enclosure' in an email. In exams, if the format is a letter, use 'Enclosure'; if email, use 'Attachment' or just mention 'I have attached…'.

Block format vs. Indented format: Block format (all lines left-aligned) is the modern standard for formal letters and what exams expect. Indented format (paragraphs indented, address/date right-aligned) is outdated. Never mix them. Use block format exclusively.
practice: Write a formal letter to the Editor of a national daily (120-150 words) about the rising problem of stray animals on city roads. Include: the issue, its dangers, and a specific call to action for municipal authorities. Use full block format with all components.

Write a job application letter (150-180 words) for the post of 'Junior Assistant' advertised in a newspaper. You are a recent graduate with computer skills. Include all block format elements and an 'Enclosure' line listing 3 documents.

Write a complaint letter (130-160 words) to the Manager of an electronics company about a washing machine purchased two weeks ago that stops mid-cycle. Include: model number, purchase date, problem description, warranty reference, and a specific remedy request with deadline.

Write an inquiry letter (100-120 words) to a travel agency asking about a package tour to Pokhara for a family of four. Ask at least 5 specific questions (cost, dates, inclusions, transport, booking process). Use proper formal tone throughout.

Identify and correct the errors in this formal letter excerpt: 'Subject: Dear Sir, I am writing to complain about the noise. I'm very angry because the construction starts at 6am. You must stop it immediately. Yours sincerely, Ram Sharma' — List at least 5 errors.
universalFacts: The block format for business letters was standardised in the 1920s by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and is now the global standard. Before that, indented and semi-block formats were common.

The 'Yours faithfully' / 'Yours sincerely' distinction originated in British civil service correspondence in the 19th century. 'Faithfully' implies loyalty to an unknown office; 'sincerely' implies genuine respect to a known individual.

In the NEB English exam, formal letter writing typically carries 8-10 marks. The marking scheme usually allocates: Format (3 marks), Content (4 marks), Expression/Tone (3 marks). Missing any format component (date, subject, salutation, close, signature) loses format marks immediately.

The word 'letter' comes from Latin 'littera' (a written character). In medieval times, letters were sealed with wax bearing the sender's signet ring — the origin of the modern 'seal' on official documents. The 'complimentary close' evolved from phrases like 'I remain your faithful servant'.

Studies show that decision-makers read the subject line and first paragraph of a formal letter most carefully. If the purpose isn't clear in the first 30 seconds, the letter is often filed or delegated. This is why exam questions emphasise a clear subject and purposeful opening.
